questions.question: Explain, using the idea of centre of gravity and base, why a tall thin object topples more easily than a short wide one, and give three ways to make a structure more stable.
questions.expected_answer: An object stays upright while the vertical line from its centre of gravity falls inside its base. A tall thin object has a high centre of gravity, so a small tilt moves it a long way sideways, and a narrow base, so the line soon falls outside it; a short wide object has a low centre of gravity and a wide base, so it must tilt much further to topple. Stability is improved by widening the base, lowering the centre of gravity by putting weight low down, and anchoring the structure with bolts or guy wires so the ground holds it.

questions.question: Describe three reinforcing techniques used on towers and explain why reinforcement is placed only where it is needed.
questions.expected_answer: A gusset is a flat, often triangular, plate fixed across a joint so members connect through a large area, spreading force and stiffening the corner. A web is a plate or lattice filling the space between two members so they act as one deeper, stiffer piece. Cross-bracing is a pair of diagonals forming an X across a panel, and internal cross-bracing through the tower's section prevents twisting. Reinforcement is targeted at joints, the lowest panels where bending is greatest and against twist, because reinforcing everywhere would make the tower heavy and expensive for no gain.

questions.question: What is visual pollution, why is it a design issue for cell phone towers, and what are three design responses with their trade-offs?
questions.expected_answer: Visual pollution is a structure spoiling the appearance of a place, such as a steel lattice dominating a residential view. It is a design issue because residents can object and a tower refused permission serves nobody, and because people affected by a structure deserve a say in its appearance. Responses: disguising the tower as a tree, steeple or flagpole, which adds cost and wind load; using a slender monopole, which uses more steel and costs more; siting it behind trees or on an industrial site, which may place it further from users; sharing one tower between networks, which makes it taller and heavier; and colouring it to fade into the background.
